items.title: Phineas Gage's recovery
items.claim: In 1848 an iron rod passed through the frontal lobe of railroad worker Phineas Gage. He survived. How long did he live afterwards?
items.reveal_title: Gage lived for roughly 12 more years
items.reveal:
Gage died in 1860 after epileptic seizures. Recent scholarship (Macmillan, 2000) suggests his personality changes were less extreme and more temporary than the textbook caricature implies.

He worked as a stagecoach driver in Chile in his later years.
items.why: Famous case studies are often simplified in retelling. Lesion evidence is more nuanced than the headline.

items.title: Type A personality's link to heart disease has weakened
items.claim: Friedman and Rosenman's 1959 'Type A' personality (competitive, impatient, hostile) was linked to coronary heart disease. What does the more recent evidence show?

options.text: Type A is the strongest predictor of heart disease
The composite Type A construct has weak predictive value in modern studies; hostility specifically (Williams 1989 onwards) retains some predictive power, while time-urgency and competitiveness do not
Type A reduces heart disease risk

items.reveal_title: Hostility, not the full Type A
items.reveal:
Friedman and Rosenman's 1976 follow-up of the Western Collaborative Group Study showed Type A nearly doubled CHD risk. Meta-analyses since the 1990s (Myrtek 2001) found weak overall effects for Type A; hostility/anger components retained predictive power.

The broader pattern: complex personality categories often decompose under empirical scrutiny into more specific traits with different effects.
items.why: Popular psychology preserves the original construct long after research has narrowed it. Specific hostility, not generic 'Type A', is what carries the cardiovascular signal.

items.title: Locus of control predicts health behaviours
items.claim: Julian Rotter's 1966 locus of control distinguishes internal (own actions cause outcomes) and external (luck, others, fate). How does it relate to health?

options.text: Locus of control has no link to health
Internal locus correlates modestly with adherence to medical regimens, exercise and other health behaviours; but it can also lead to self-blame when illness occurs despite effort

items.reveal:
Wallston's Multidimensional Health Locus of Control scale (1978) refined Rotter's construct for health applications. Meta-analyses (Norman et al. 1998) find modest correlations between internal HLOC and health behaviours.

Caveats: structural factors (income, access to care, environment) often dwarf locus of control's effect. Heavy 'personal responsibility' framing can ignore upstream determinants of health.
items.why: Individual-level psychological variables matter for health behaviours but operate within structural constraints. Both levels of analysis are needed.
